items.prose: A pre-trade risk check tests $H_0$: the order is safe. It blocks an order that was in fact safe.
items.question: Which error has the check made?

options.why: A type II error lets a bad order through. Here a safe order was blocked.

options.text: No error: blocking is the cautious choice
options.why: Caution has a cost. Rejecting a true $H_0$ is an error whatever the motive.
Power is about catching bad orders. This order was safe.

feedback.correct: A true $H_0$ was rejected: type I.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which hypothesis was true and what the check decided.

explain.text: The order was safe, so $H_0$ was true, and the check rejected it. That is a type I error, a false alarm.

items.prose: Strategy X: 200 days, mean 0.12% a day, sd 0.8%. Strategy Y: 150 days, mean 0.05%, sd 1.2%. They trade unrelated markets.
items.question: What is Welch's $t$ for X minus Y?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each sd, divide by its own $n$, add, then take the root.

byKey.no-n: You divided the gap by $\sqrt{s_X^2 + s_Y^2}$ without the $n$s.

items.prose: A one-sided 5% test of mean 0. The true mean is 0.1 with sd 0.8, and $n = 144$. Useful values: $\Phi(-0.145) = 0.442$, $\Phi(0.145) = 0.558$.
items.question: What is the power?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma$, subtract 1.645, then use $\Phi$.

byKey.beta: 0.558 is $\beta$, the chance of missing the effect.

explain.text: $\delta\sqrt n/\sigma = 0.1 \times 12/0.8 = 1.5$, just short of the cut-off. Power $= \Phi(1.5 - 1.645) = \Phi(-0.145) = 0.442$: the test misses this effect more often than not.

items.prose: A broker tests a routing change on 2 million trades. It improves fills by 0.001 bp on average, with $p < 0.0001$.
items.question: What should the desk conclude?

options.text: The gain is almost surely real but too small to matter
A $p$ this small means a big improvement
options.why: $p$ mixes size with sample size. Two million trades make a tiny gain significant.

options.text: There is a 99.99% chance the change pays for itself
options.why: $1 - p$ is not a chance about the change, and 0.001 bp is less than any cost.

options.text: The result must be a mistake
options.why: Nothing is wrong: with $n$ this large, every true difference becomes significant.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate how sure we are from how big the gain is.

explain.text: With 2 million trades the standard error is tiny, so even 0.001 bp is many standard errors from 0. Significance says the gain is probably not zero. It says nothing about whether it is worth having.

items.prose: The desk's test has $z$ centred at 2.5 under $H_1$. It loosens the cut-off from 1.645 to 1.282, so $\alpha$ rises to 0.10. Useful value: $\Phi(-1.218) = 0.112$.
items.question: What is $\beta$ now?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\beta = \Phi(c - m)$ with the new cut-off.

explain.text: $\beta = \Phi(1.282 - 2.5) = \Phi(-1.218) = 0.112$. Doubling $\alpha$ from 0.05 to 0.10 cut $\beta$ from 0.196 to 0.112.

items.prose: Ten pairs of days compare two hedging rules on the same days. The daily cost saved has mean $\bar d = 1.2$ bp and sd $s_d = 1.5$ bp.
items.question: What is the paired $t$ statistic?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The standard error of $\bar d$ is $s_d/\sqrt{10}$.

byKey.no-root: You divided by $s_d$ alone. Divide by $s_d/\sqrt{10}$.

explain.text: SE $= 1.5/\sqrt{10} = 0.474$, so $t = 1.2/0.474 = 2.53$, and the two-sided $p$ with 9 df is 0.032.

items.prose: Only 5% of the ideas a team tests are real. Its tests have power 0.6 at $\alpha = 0.05$. One idea comes back significant.
items.question: What is $P(\text{real} \mid \text{significant})$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the real passes against the noise passes.

byKey.one-minus-alpha: $1 - \alpha$ ignores the base rate. Most ideas here are noise.
byKey.power: 0.6 is $P(\text{sig} \mid \text{real})$, the reverse of what is asked.
byKey.prior: 0.05 is the base rate before the test. A significant result should raise it.

explain.text: Real passes: $0.05 \times 0.6 = 0.03$. Noise passes: $0.95 \times 0.05 = 0.0475$. So $P(\text{real} \mid \text{sig}) = 0.03/0.0775 = 0.387$; in odds, $12 \times 1{:}19 = 12{:}19$.

items.prose: A strategy has true mean daily return 0.04% and daily sd 1.2%. We want 80% power in a one-sided 5% test of mean 0. Use $n = 6.18\,(\sigma/\delta)^2$.
items.question: How many trading days are needed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\sigma/\delta = 1.2/0.04 = 30$; square it and multiply by 6.18.

byKey.no-square: You multiplied by $\sigma/\delta$ without squaring it.
byKey.flipped: You used $\delta/\sigma$. A small edge needs more days, not fewer.

explain.text: $\sigma/\delta = 30$, so $n = 6.18 \times 900 \approx 5{,}562$ days, about 22 years. No real backtest of this strategy could have 80% power.
